title: Paul Defends the Gospel Received from Christ
summary_text: Paul says his work as an apostle comes from Jesus Christ and God, not people. He rebukes the Galatians for leaving Christ's grace for a false gospel and puts its preachers under a curse. His gospel came from Christ's revelation, not human teaching. Once a fierce enemy of the church, he was called by God to preach His Son among Gentiles. He describes his early travels and brief contact with apostles, while churches praised God for his changed life.
key_points: Paul's apostleship comes from Jesus Christ and God, and Jesus gave Himself to rescue people from their sins and this evil age.
Paul condemns any gospel that contradicts the one the Galatians received, even if an angel proclaims it.
Paul received his gospel from Jesus Christ by revelation, despite his former efforts to destroy God's church.
Paul first went to Arabia and Damascus, then later visited Cephas and saw James in Jerusalem.
The churches of Judea glorified God on hearing that their former persecutor now preached the faith.

title: The Gospel and Justification Through Faith
summary_text: Jerusalem's leaders accept Paul's gospel to Gentiles without forcing Titus to be circumcised. Paul later confronts Cephas for refusing to eat with Gentiles out of fear, drawing others into hypocrisy. People are justified by faith in Christ, not works of the law, and Christ does not promote sin. Paul describes himself as crucified with Christ and living by faith in the Son of God. He will not set aside grace, since righteousness through law would make Christ's death pointless.
key_points: Paul resists pressure to circumcise Titus so that the gospel's truth and freedom in Christ remain intact.
The leaders recognize Paul's apostleship to the uncircumcised and ask him to remember the poor.
Paul says Cephas stood condemned and confronts his refusal to eat with Gentiles, which drew others into hypocrisy.
People are justified by faith in Christ rather than works of the law, and Christ does not promote sin.
Paul lives by faith in God's Son, declaring that righteousness through law would make Christ's death pointless.

title: Abraham's Promise and Faith in Christ
summary_text: The Galatians received the Spirit through faith, so Paul challenges their turn to works of the law. God credited Abraham's faith as righteousness, and Christ redeemed people from the law's curse to bring blessing to Gentiles. The later law cannot cancel God's covenant or His promise to Abraham's seed, Christ. It was added because of transgressions and guarded people under sin until they could be justified by faith. Those baptized into Christ are sons of God, united in Him and heirs of Abraham's promise.
key_points: Having heard Christ presented as crucified and received the Spirit through faith, the Galatians now turn toward the flesh.
The gospel announced blessing for Gentiles through Abraham, whose faith God credited as righteousness.
Christ redeemed people by taking the law's curse, bringing Abraham's blessing and the promised Spirit through faith.
The law does not cancel God's covenant; it was added because of transgressions and served as a guardian until Christ.
Baptized believers are sons of God, united in Christ and heirs of Abraham's promise.

title: Sons and Heirs Rather Than Slaves
summary_text: God sent His Son to redeem those under law and give them adoption as sons and heirs. His Son's Spirit cries to the Father from their hearts, so Paul asks why they want slavery again. He recalls their care when illness brought him to preach the gospel and longs for Christ to be formed in them. Using Abraham's sons, Paul compares two covenants: Hagar means slavery, while the Jerusalem above is free. He calls believers children of promise like Isaac, born by the Spirit and belonging to the free woman.
key_points: God sent His Son to redeem those under law, giving them adoption and the Spirit who cries to the Father.
Paul fears that observing days and seasons marks a return to the slavery the Galatians left.
Paul recalls their care during his illness and warns that others seek to separate them from him.
Paul makes Hagar and the free woman illustrations of two covenants, contrasting slavery with the freedom of Jerusalem above.
Like Isaac, believers are children of promise, persecuted by those born of the flesh but belonging to the free woman's inheritance.

title: Freedom in Christ and the Spirit's Fruit
summary_text: Paul warns that seeking to be justified through circumcision cuts people off from Christ and grace. He points instead to faith active in love. Freedom means serving others in love, not feeding the flesh, which fights against the Spirit. Acts such as sexual sin, idolatry, and hatred keep those practicing them from the kingdom of God. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, while the Spirit bears fruit such as love, joy, and peace.
key_points: By the Spirit, believers await the hope of righteousness through faith; circumcision and uncircumcision have no value beside faith active in love.
Paul says the teachers disturbing them will face judgment and rejects their pressure for circumcision.
Called to freedom, believers must serve others in love, fulfilling the law's command to love one's neighbor.
The Spirit and flesh oppose each other, and those practicing the flesh's sinful acts will not inherit God's kingdom.
The Spirit's fruit includes faithfulness and self-control, and believers must follow the Spirit without conceit or envy.

title: Bearing Burdens and Boasting in the Cross
summary_text: Paul urges gentle care for anyone caught in a trespass, shared burdens, and honest judgment of one's own work. Sowing to the flesh brings ruin, while sowing to the Spirit brings eternal life, so believers must keep doing good. Those pressing circumcision want to avoid suffering and boast about others. Paul boasts only in Christ's cross, which has crucified him to the world, and says what matters is a new creation, not circumcision or uncircumcision. He closes with peace, mercy, and grace.
key_points: Gentle care and shared burdens fulfill Christ's law, while each person must examine his own work.
Paul urges support for teachers of the word and warns that sowing to flesh or Spirit brings destruction or eternal life.
Believers must persist in doing good, especially toward others in the family of faith.
Paul rejects boasting in circumcision and boasts only in Christ's cross, emphasizing the new creation.
Paul blesses those following this rule, points to Jesus' marks on his body, and closes with grace.
